text: The Taliban published an 11-page biography of Mullah Mohammed Omar, claiming he remains the group's leader, in an apparent effort to dispel rumors of his death. The document, released on the 19th anniversary of the Taliban's founding, also seeks to reassert Omar's jihadi credentials amid a leadership challenge from ISIS's self-declared caliph. Omar, who has not been seen or heard from in years, is described as overseeing the Taliban's leadership council and military commanders across Afghanistan.

Hundreds of mourners attended the South Carolina funeral of Walter Scott, the unarmed black man fatally shot in the back by a white police officer, with speakers calling his death a catalyst for change in America. Officer Michael Slager has been charged with murder and fired over the shooting, which was captured on bystander video. A witness has described a scuffle before the shooting, and a defense attorney said the charge could be reduced to manslaughter.

A former TSA agent was sentenced to six months in jail and five and a half years of probation for secretly recording a female co-worker in a bathroom and burglarizing her home. Police found over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on Daniel Boykin's devices. He pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and a computer act violation.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost economic development, lacking conventional natural resources like oil and gold. The Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo aim to expose Cape Verdean artists internationally, with tourism expected to reach 20% of GDP by 2024. Despite early promise, the UN notes the creative sector remains a small part of the economy with room for growth.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to stay second in the Premier League, moving within four points of leaders Chelsea, who have two games in hand. Aaron Ramsey scored the winner as Arsenal extended their winning run to eight matches. At the bottom, Aston Villa, Leicester and Crystal Palace all won, while Sunderland lost 4-1 at home.

Original Twin Peaks cast members have launched a #SaveTwinPeaks video campaign backing David Lynch in his salary dispute with Showtime. Lynch exited the nine-episode revival Sunday over insufficient funding. Showtime says it still hopes to revive the series with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Andrew Getty, 47, heir to the Getty oil fortune, appears to have died of natural causes at his Los Angeles home, police said. The coroner's preliminary assessment found no foul play, and an autopsy is planned. Getty, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, had "several health issues," and no criminal investigation is underway.

A Maryland woman accused of abandoning her quadriplegic son in a Philadelphia park for days cannot be extradited to face charges until she completes unspecified treatment, police said. Nyia Parler, 41, was taken into custody Sunday after her 21-year-old son was found Friday in Cobbs Creek Park with a Bible and wheelchair nearby. She faces aggravated assault and related charges once extradited.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Nobel Peace Prize winner Malala Yousafzai. Asteroid 316201 Malala, roughly 4 kilometers in diameter, orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter. Mainzer said she wanted to honor the education activist because few asteroids are named for women.

Gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 people aboard the Celebrity Infinity, including 95 of 2,117 passengers and five of 964 crew members, the CDC reports. The cause is unknown; two CDC staffers will meet the ship Monday in San Diego. It is the ship's third such outbreak, after 2006 and 2013.

"Star Wars" went digital, Mindy Kaling's brother admitted faking his race for medical school, and actor James Best died. A Burger-King couple got a free wedding, Michelle Obama danced, and Nina Dobrev left "The Vampire Diaries."

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman Thursday with attempting to travel overseas to join ISIS, one of three women arrested this week on terror charges. Keonna Thomas, 30, allegedly purchased a ticket to Barcelona via Turkey after posting pro-ISIS messages on social media. Two New York women were also arrested for allegedly plotting to build an explosive device for US attacks.

HBO released a teaser for "True Detective" Season 2, premiering June 21 with Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch. The plot follows three law-enforcement officers and a career criminal entangled in a murder conspiracy across California. Season 1, starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, was a ratings hit.

Carlos Colina, 32, was charged Monday after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and additional body parts were discovered at a nearby apartment building. The remains were identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who authorities say knew Colina. Colina was arraigned on charges of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury and improper disposal of a body.

A Kentucky high school basketball star bound for Ball State has asked a freshman with Down syndrome to his prom, and the viral prom-posal has drawn widespread attention. Trey Moses invited Ellie Meredith in her gym class with flowers and a Taylor Swift-themed poster, after getting her parents' approval. Ellie's mother says the invitation has been a relief for her daughter, who has struggled with friendships since elementary school.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week sequel to the History Channel's hit "The Bible," on Easter Sunday. It's one of six shows to watch this week, along with the final episodes of "Mad Men," new series "American Odyssey" and "The Comedians," the return of "Louie," and Netflix's "Marvel's Daredevil."

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed a religious freedom law that critics say permits discrimination against gays and lesbians, drawing national backlash. The move was aimed at shoring up his conservative credentials ahead of a possible 2016 presidential run. The controversy is forcing Republican hopefuls to take positions on similar "religious freedom" bills advancing in other red states.

Apple released a new iOS version with more diverse emojis, including a range of skin tones and same-sex couple options. The update drew both praise for greater inclusivity and criticism, with some groups like redheads and Armenians noting they were still left out.

Singer Avril Lavigne revealed to People magazine that she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease, which she believes she got from a tick bite last spring. The 30-year-old, who said she is now "80 percent better," is releasing a new single this month to support the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research from the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and Margot Frank died at least a month earlier than the previously recorded date of March 31, 1945. Researchers concluded the sisters likely succumbed to a typhus outbreak at Bergen-Belsen before February 7, 1945, based on survivor testimonies and re-examined archives. The exact dates of their deaths remain unknown, with Margot dying before Anne.

Two Troy University students were arrested and charged with gang rape after allegedly assaulting a woman during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. Authorities discovered video of the March 2015 incident during an unrelated shooting investigation. Both men have been suspended from school, and more arrests are expected.

A stray dog in Washington State survived being hit by a car, struck in the head with a hammer and buried in a field, then staggered to a nearby farm four days later. The one-year-old bully breed mix, now named Theia, is receiving care at Washington State University's veterinary hospital for a dislocated jaw, leg injuries and a caved-in sinus cavity. A fundraising page for her treatment has surpassed its $10,000 target.

The FBI has confirmed that Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a January raid in the Philippines. The raid, which targeted Marwan in Maguindanao province, left 44 Philippine police commandos dead and shattered a ceasefire with the MILF. The FBI had offered a $5 million reward for Marwan, a Jemaah Islamiyah member accused of supplying IEDs and training terror groups.

The Obama administration's nuclear framework with Iran grants sanctions relief and preserves enrichment capacity while lacking anytime-anywhere inspections, critics say. Congress's tougher sanctions bill, which passed the House 400-20, was blocked in the Senate. Opponents warn Iran could cheat and "sneak out" to a bomb, as North Korea did after a similar 1994 deal.

"Mad Men" begins its final season Sunday, ending an eight-year run that made the 1960s ad agency drama a cultural touchstone despite modest ratings. The final episodes are expected to cover late 1969 into 1970, with creator Matthew Weiner keeping plot details secret. The show's characters face disintegration as the era's old orders collapse.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a 6-foot-tall calf Friday evening in an hour-long labor streamed live by Animal Planet. The newborn's gender and condition were not immediately known, but it was seen moving its ears, attempting to stand and trying to nurse. The calf joins a 4-year-old sister, Jamie.

Loretta Lynch's nomination as the first African-American woman attorney general has been pending a full Senate vote for over six months, longer than the eight previous attorney general nominees combined. Senate Republicans deny racial motivations for the delay, attributing it to partisan disputes over a human trafficking bill and Obama's 2014 immigration actions. Lynch's family and supporters in Durham, North Carolina, cite her civil rights roots and allege race is a factor in the stalled confirmation.

Three killed, five wounded after armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in Afghanistan's Balkh province Thursday. Two police officers and a security guard were among the dead. A firefight between Afghan security forces and the attackers is ongoing.

Bob Barker returned to "The Price Is Right" on April 1, hosting the first game for the first time since 2007. The 91-year-old handled "Lucky Seven" before handing duties to Drew Carey. Barker appeared spry and didn't miss a beat.

Blues legend B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration caused by his Type II diabetes but has since been released. The 89-year-old guitarist said he is "feeling much better" and is back home resting with his grandchildren. King suffered a similar dehydration episode last year that forced him to cancel the rest of his tour.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The verdict was expected, but the deeper question is how to prevent future radicalization among young Muslims. Understanding and countering radicalization—not reforming Islam—is key to preventing future violence.

This week's top videos include a tour of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, a ride on the world's tallest giga-coaster, and a CNN exclusive interview with a former Bikram yoga student alleging sexual assault. Other highlights: a shepherd's account of the Germanwings crash, a heated panel on Indiana's religious freedom law, and a physics professor's composite of beautiful faces.

The Pentagon says coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory seized by ISIS, with gains concentrated in central and northern Iraq. A counterinsurgency expert cautions that territorial gains are fluid, and ISIS is compensating for losses with high-profile attacks elsewhere to sustain its image of momentum.

An Air Canada passenger on a Toronto-to-Atlanta flight was attacked Friday when a man seated behind him tried to choke him with a cord about 30 minutes before landing. The suspect was escorted off the plane in Atlanta and taken for mental evaluation; no federal charges are pending. The victim, Ottawa Fury FC player Oliver Minatel, was unharmed and is set to play Saturday.

Hong Kong police found two women's bodies in a Wan Chai apartment last November after Briton Rurik Jutting, 29, called them to the scene. Jutting, a former Bank of America Merrill Lynch trader, was charged with two counts of murder. A court hearing to determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed to trial was adjourned Thursday until May.

One person died in Fairdale, Illinois, as multiple tornadoes struck the rural Midwest Thursday, part of a two-day outbreak that also spawned twisters in Iowa and near St. Louis. The Ogle County sheriff said 20 homes were destroyed and 50 to 100 significantly damaged, though injuries were treatable. Eight tornadoes were reported Wednesday in Oklahoma, Kansas and Missouri.

Don McLean's handwritten lyrics for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's Tuesday, the third-highest auction price for an American literary manuscript. McLean, who turns 70 this year, said he sold the 16-page draft to secure his family's future. The 1972 No. 1 hit remains one of pop music's most dissected songs.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit Saturday to the Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp in Syria to assess the humanitarian situation. The camp, largely cut off from aid since November 2013, is home to about 18,000 Palestinians and Syrian civilians, including 3,500 children, and remains under the control of armed groups including ISIS and Al-Nusra Front. Krähenbühl will meet with Syrian officials, UN staff and displaced camp residents.

Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and ground fighting in Yemen have killed an estimated 600 people in just over a week, with Houthi rebels still controlling Sanaa despite heavy infrastructure damage and power outages affecting 16 million residents. The ICRC has called for a humanitarian ceasefire to deliver medical aid, but a supply flight remains grounded in Djibouti, while the UN Security Council adjourned without action on a Russian draft resolution to halt the strikes. Deposed President Hadi, holed up in Saudi Arabia, fired his former army chief of staff in a move with no practical effect, as AQAP exploits the chaos to expand its control in eastern Yemen.

Richie Benaud, former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster, has died at 84. Benaud, who said last year he was being treated for skin cancer, was revered for his witty commentary and record-breaking playing career. Tributes poured in from Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott and cricketers worldwide.

A total lunar eclipse will be visible across western North America early Saturday, lasting four minutes and 43 seconds—the shortest of the century. The eclipse begins at 3:16 a.m. PT, with totality at 4:58 a.m. PT; partial views are possible nationwide, though East Coast sunrise will interrupt it. Parts of South America, India, China and Russia can also see it, but Europe, Africa and the Middle East cannot.

A federal grand jury indicted Robert Durst, 71, on a charge of unlawful firearm possession after a .38-caliber revolver was allegedly found in his New Orleans hotel room last month. Durst, already held without bail on a first-degree murder charge in California, faces up to 10 years in prison on the new charge. He also faces state weapons and drug charges in New Orleans and awaits extradition to Los Angeles in the 2000 killing of Susan Berman.

"Furious 7" opens Friday, offering fans a chance to mourn Paul Walker, who died in a 2013 car crash at age 40 during a break from filming. Producers rewrote the script and used Walker's brothers as body doubles rather than kill off his character, Brian O'Connor. Co-star Vin Diesel and others have paid tribute to Walker, praised as one of Hollywood's nicest guys.

A "Price Is Right" model accidentally revealed the answer to a car-guessing game, handing a contestant a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey laughed it off, and the model later tweeted that all was fine. The mishap capped a busy week that included Bob Barker's return to the show.

Thai Smile, a subsidiary of Thai Airways, unveiled an Adventure Time-themed Airbus A320 at Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi International Airport, featuring Jake, Finn and Princess Bubblegum on the exterior and show characters throughout the interior. The plane results from a partnership between Thai Smile and Cartoon Network Amazone, a new water park near Pattaya. Its inaugural flight runs from Bangkok to Phuket on April 4.

CNN's Brian Todd and photojournalist Khalil Abdallah encountered a brood of ducklings and their mother crossing a busy Washington street on Tuesday. Pedestrians, including a man who donated his umbrella, helped corral the ducks and stop traffic so they could cross safely. The birds were relocated to a grassy area at 16th and L streets NW.

Investigators have finished collecting evidence at the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site and are not expected to return. A private security firm will guard the site until remaining debris is removed. All 150 people on board were killed when co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane.

Cuba and the U.S. are attending the Summit of the Americas together for the first time since 1962, with Washington expected to announce Cuba's removal from its state sponsor of terrorism list as early as this week. The historic thaw could pave the way for re-establishing formal relations and reopening embassies, though Cuba's ties to Venezuela and a street brawl between Cuban officials and dissidents in Panama underscore lingering tensions.

Jesus and his disciples relied on donations and hospitality to fund their ministry, operating at a subsistence level. Women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna, along with wealthy supporters such as Joseph of Arimathea, provided for them out of their own resources. The Jesus community maintained a common purse to survive, as evidenced by Judas' objection to Mary's costly anointing.

California regulators fined Pacific Gas & Electric $1.6 billion Thursday for unsafe operation of its gas transmission system, including a 2010 pipeline rupture in San Bruno that killed eight people. Most of the record penalty—$850 million—is earmarked for pipeline safety infrastructure improvements, with $50 million for other safety remedies. PG&E CEO Tony Earley said the company is working to become the safest energy company in the US and has already paid more than $500 million in victim claims.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old brain cancer patient who inspired millions by playing in a college basketball game, has died. Hill, who was diagnosed with an inoperable tumor in 2013, raised $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research and became a worldwide symbol of perseverance. She died early Friday, her school announced.

A four-alarm fire broke out Friday morning at the General Electric Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke and flames over the industrial site. No injuries or trapped people were reported. The cause is unknown and firefighters are spraying water from the periphery.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, a key figure in nuclear talks with the U.S., received a hero's welcome upon returning to Iran. Lesser-known facts about Zarif include his 2013 Rosh Hashanah tweet disavowing Holocaust denial, his education and family ties in the U.S., and his involvement in the 1979 takeover of the Iranian Consulate in San Francisco.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to return a 17-year-old girl in state custody to her mother's home while she completes court-ordered chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. The teen, identified as Cassandra C., is in remission after nearly six months of treatment and is expected to finish this month. Her attorneys say they are weighing another appeal.

New research suggests "Double Falsehood," a play published in 1728 by Lewis Theobald, was actually written by William Shakespeare with help from John Fletcher. Two University of Texas scholars used computer software to analyze the language of all three men and found a "landslide" match between the play and Shakespeare. The study, published in Psychological Science, may settle a long-running debate over the play's authorship.

Marseille prosecutor Brice Robin denies any video from Germanwings Flight 9525 is part of the investigation, after Bild and Paris Match claimed to have cell phone footage of the final seconds. French gendarmerie spokesman Lt. Col. Jean-Marc Menichini called the reports "completely wrong," saying recovered cell phones have not yet been analyzed. Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz disclosed a "previous episode of severe depression" in 2009 and was allowed to continue training.

American Samoan veteran Emy Afalava is suing the federal government for denying him citizenship and voting rights despite his birth on U.S. soil, a case now before the D.C. Circuit. The Fourteenth Amendment grants citizenship to all persons born in U.S. jurisdictions, yet American Samoans remain the only inhabitants of a U.S. island territory still denied that right. The lawsuit seeks to overturn a century-old legacy of racially motivated rulings that have excluded islanders from full citizenship.

Blue Bell has temporarily shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, ice cream plant after listeria was found in a serving produced there. The CDC warned consumers not to eat certain 3-ounce Blue Bell cups made at the plant, though other Blue Bell products are unaffected. The move marks the company's third action amid a listeria outbreak linked to a Kansas hospital.

Al-Shabaab claimed an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya, killing many and taking hostages. The assault marks an escalation of the group's cross-border raids and signals deteriorating security in East Africa.

The US is protesting to Moscow after a Russian Su-27 intercepted a US RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in what the Pentagon called an "unsafe and unprofessional" manner. Russia claims the US aircraft had its transponder off and was approaching the Russian border, which US officials deny. The Pentagon and State Department will file a formal complaint through diplomatic channels.

A hooded angel with black wings, created by artist Phillip Hyman, appeared near the site of Walter Scott's fatal shooting in North Charleston and became an icon of the Black Lives Matter movement. Hyman crafted the piece from reclaimed wood as a way to mourn with Scott's family. Protesters have since adopted the artwork for demonstrations at City Hall.

Eyewitness video of white North Charleston police Officer Michael Slager fatally shooting unarmed black man Walter Scott contradicts initial police reports that Scott took Slager's Taser. Slager, fired and charged with murder, shot Scott eight times as he ran away; the witness says Scott never grabbed the Taser. The police report's accounts from eight officers differ on details including whether CPR was performed.

ISIS claimed Sunday it controlled part of Iraq's largest oil refinery after launching an assault on the Baiji facility late Saturday. Iraqi officials denied the claim, insisting government forces remain in full control. CNN could not independently verify either side's account.

Nashville's DA banned sterilization in plea deals after prosecutors offered it four times in five years, sparking outrage. Similar deals are common nationwide, mostly for men, and likely constitutional if voluntarily accepted. The outrage may stem from gender bias, as sterilizing women feels more cruel than sterilizing men.

More than 25,000 people contracted Ebola over the past year and over 10,000 died, with dozens still newly infected each week, according to the latest WHO report. The epidemic, the worst in history, exposed flaws in government health systems, though case numbers have fallen sharply in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Guinea remains a concern, with unknown chains of transmission possibly fueling new infections.

The NCAA claims in a court filing it has no legal duty to ensure student-athletes receive an education, despite years of public messaging that academics come first. The filing responds to a lawsuit by former UNC athletes over the largest academic fraud scandal in NCAA history. Critics call the position double talk, noting the NCAA has similarly disclaimed legal responsibility for athlete health and safety.

An explosion at a controversial chemical plant in southeastern China's Fujian province injured six people and sparked a large fire Monday night. The Zhangzhou plant produces paraxylene (PX), a potentially carcinogenic chemical used in polyester production. More than 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control; the plant was previously hit by an explosion in 2013.

A defense attorney argues the bystander video of Walter Scott's shooting death shows the necessity of police body cameras. He contends cameras would deter excessive force, reduce complaints, and help break the cycle of mistrust between police and minority communities. He also calls for addressing deeper racial bias in the criminal justice system.

The Summit of the Americas in Panama City was expected to center on a historic U.S.-Cuba handshake, but Venezuela's presence created a "triangle of tension." Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro accused the U.S. of coup plotting and rallied Latin American allies, while Obama sanctioned seven Venezuelan officials. Cuba publicly sided with Maduro, complicating the summit for Washington.

A nuclear submarine caught fire at a Russian shipyard in northwestern Russia, state media reported. The fire was caused by rubber insulation igniting during welding work, with no ammunition or nuclear fuel aboard. No injuries were reported and the fire posed no threat, officials said.

Tropical storm Maysak, known locally as Chedeng, is approaching the Philippines, prompting warnings for flash floods and landslides. Once a super typhoon, it has weakened but still carries winds over 70 mph and gusts up to 90 mph. Preemptive evacuations and activity bans are in place as the storm is expected to make landfall Sunday in Isabela province.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly scolded his son, Deion Sanders Jr., on Twitter for claiming he only eats "hood doughnuts." The elder Sanders reminded his 912,000 followers that his son has a trust fund, a condo and his own clothing line. Sanders Jr., a SMU wide receiver, retweeted his father's rebuke.

Gender-based violence is at epidemic levels in Guatemala, which ranks third worldwide in killings of women, with two women murdered daily and 98% of cases never reaching court. A legacy of civil war atrocities, entrenched impunity, machismo culture, and weak institutions fuel the violence. Despite slow reforms and NGO efforts, millions of Guatemalan women remain trapped in a cycle of abuse.

Police in Malegaon, Maharashtra, are requiring residents to submit photos and "unique features" of their cattle to enforce the state's new beef ban. Over 100 owners have complied; officials say the database will help solve cow slaughter cases. Beef traders ended a month-long strike and vowed to challenge the law in court.

Lucknow police have purchased four pepper-spraying drones, costing up to $19,300 each, to disperse violent protests and mob attacks. The measure has drawn mixed reactions, with critics citing free speech concerns and a preference for dialogue over force. The drones are set to be officially launched later this month.

Christie's sold the 16-page handwritten manuscript of Don McLean's "American Pie" lyrics for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer on Tuesday. The 8½-minute song, released in 1971, remains one of the most enduring works of American pop music.

A daring Easter weekend raid on a London vault in the jewelry district saw thieves crack dozens of safety deposit boxes, an "Ocean's 11"-style heist not seen in the city for over 40 years. Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm explains that such sophisticated jobs require meticulous planning, inside information and tight-knit teams, unlike typical burglaries. Detectives will scrutinize inside involvement, forensic evidence and known criminal networks in a relentless investigation.

7-Eleven is hosting its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day at US stores Saturday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., letting customers fill a container of their choice for $1.49. Cups must be sanitary and fit within a 10-inch-diameter hole; garbage cans are not allowed. The event is separate from the traditional Free Slurpee Day on July 11.

Kentucky State Sen. Georgia Davis Powers criticizes Rand Paul's presidential campaign launch, saying his record on civil rights and voting rights is disqualifying. Powers, the first woman and person of color elected to the Kentucky State Senate, says Paul's minority outreach is undermined by his opposition to the Civil Rights Act, Voting Rights Act and other policies. She says the American people deserve better than Paul.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at Walt Disney World Speedway's Exotic Driving Experience on Sunday, killing passenger Gary Terry, 36. The driver, Tavon Watson, 24, lost control and was hospitalized with minor injuries. Operator Petty Holdings extended sympathies.

The defense rested Monday in the Aaron Hernandez murder trial after calling witnesses for less than a day, following months of prosecution testimony from 131 witnesses. Closing arguments are set for Tuesday, after which the jury will deliberate in the circumstantial case over the June 2013 shooting death of Odin Lloyd. Hernandez, 25, has pleaded not guilty.

Chinese authorities have formally detained women's rights activist Wu Rongrong and four others on charges of "creating disturbances" after their March detention for planning an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment. Supporters were briefly detained and an NGO raided, with the five facing release or formal arrest by April 13. The crackdown comes as Beijing prepares to mark the 20th anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women and consider its first anti-domestic violence law.

Martin O'Malley said Friday in Iowa that Hillary Clinton's inevitability as Democratic frontrunner is not unbreakable, citing her 2008 loss to Barack Obama. The former Maryland governor, polling in low single digits, has teased a presidential run while avoiding direct attacks on Clinton. Clinton plans to launch her candidacy Sunday via social media video.

Ursula Ward, mother of Odin Lloyd, testified Wednesday at the sentencing of Aaron Hernandez, who was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison for Lloyd's June 2013 killing. Lloyd's family described him as a hardworking, gifted athlete and devoted family man. Ward said she forgives those involved in her son's murder.

Ted Cruz courted Iowa evangelicals during his first presidential campaign swing, emphasizing religious liberty and faith in a bid to energize the state's influential Christian right. Cruz, the only declared GOP candidate, is pursuing a three-pronged strategy targeting evangelicals, tea party supporters and libertarians. He faces likely competition for the evangelical vote from Mike Huckabee and Rick Santorum, the past two Iowa caucus winners.

Marvel revealed the Vision (Paul Bettany) via poster ahead of "Avengers: Age of Ultron," plus a first look at Charlie Cox's Daredevil suit. Bryan Singer announced Ben Hardy as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse," and the new "Fantastic Four" Thing was unveiled. The flurry of superhero reveals signals the genre's continued dominance.

Italy's coast guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean on Friday, picking them up 30 miles off Libya. More than 10,000 migrants have reached Italy in the first three months of 2015, and at least 480 have died crossing the Mediterranean this year, up sharply from fewer than 50 at this time last year. Most come from West Africa, Somalia and Syria, using Libya as a transit country.

French-language network TV5Monde regained control of one of its 11 channels Thursday after a crippling cyberattack halted broadcasts and social media. The network said it was "hacked by an Islamist group," and ISIS logos appeared on its accounts, though no group claimed responsibility. TV5Monde reaches 260 million homes worldwide.

David Lynch says he won't direct the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient pay from Showtime. The network said it was "saddened" and hopes to resolve remaining deal points to bring back the show with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

High-profile trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev near their conclusions in Massachusetts. Rand Paul announces his presidential candidacy in Kentucky, while Chicago holds its first mayoral runoff and Ferguson, Missouri, votes amid racial tensions.

Tornado sirens sounded in Kansas Wednesday night as severe storms spawned reported twisters, including one near Goddard that missed Wichita. Tornadoes were also reported in southwestern Kansas and possibly in Potosi, Missouri, where wind damage and flooding occurred. More storms are expected Thursday across the Midwest, Mississippi and Tennessee river valleys, and near the southern Great Lakes.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release Monday for the 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. The sentence was handed down by Judge Sherry Stephens after two juries deadlocked on the death penalty. Arias expressed remorse before sentencing.

The EPA says a harmful pesticide, methyl bromide, was present in a U.S. Virgin Islands villa where a Delaware family of four fell ill and was hospitalized after renting the unit in March. The pesticide is banned for indoor use in the U.S., and the EPA is investigating whether fumigation at the resort violated environmental laws. The Justice Department has opened a criminal probe, and Terminix, which provided pest control, says it is cooperating.

A Columbia Journalism School review found Rolling Stone's article about an alleged gang rape at the University of Virginia was the product of "an institutional failure" spanning reporting, editing, supervision and fact-checking. Managing editor Will Dana apologized to readers and to those damaged by the story, including the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity and UVA administrators and students. Legal experts say UVA cannot sue for defamation, but fraternity members could pursue a rare successful case if they clear procedural hurdles and show tangible damages.

FBI agents and task force officers confronted armed robbery suspect Kevone Charleston in a Forsyth County, Georgia, CVS parking lot Saturday morning. Charleston rammed multiple government vehicles while fleeing, injuring two agents, before being shot and captured. Charleston is suspected in 32 commercial robberies dating to November 2013.

An Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle shortly after takeoff Monday after a ramp agent was found asleep in the cargo hold, prompting banging heard by passengers and crew. The man, a Menzies Aviation contractor, was unharmed and taken to a hospital as a precaution. The flight later resumed and reached Los Angeles; Alaska Airlines is investigating.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks, charged in the February shooting deaths of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill, is eligible for the death penalty. Hicks, 46, was indicted on three counts of first-degree murder and one count of discharging a firearm into an occupied dwelling. Police cited an ongoing parking dispute as a possible factor but have not dismissed a hate crime; the Justice Department opened a parallel preliminary inquiry.

Amnesty International's report "Their Lives on the Line" urges authorities to address attacks on Afghan women's rights activists, who face persecution from the Taliban, warlords, and government officials. The report follows the brutal mob killing of Farkhunda in Kabul, where women served as pallbearers for the first time, and cites U.N. figures showing a 20% rise in women killed in 2013. Amnesty says the Afghan government has done little to protect activists, with perpetrators rarely prosecuted.

A New York judge authorized divorce papers to be served via Facebook private message. The ruling reflects the evolution of service of process law, which increasingly accepts online methods as more reliable than traditional alternatives like publication or "nail and mail." Online service offers tracking benefits and may become more common as people live more of their lives on the internet.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" television ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, died Thursday at 88 after battling esophageal cancer. Schuller, who preached a "possibility thinking" message from a drive-in theater to a global television audience, saw his ministry file for bankruptcy in 2010 amid a family succession dispute.

Four workers were killed and 45 injured in an oil rig fire off Mexico's coast Wednesday. Pemex evacuated about 300 workers from the Abkatun Permanente platform; the blaze was extinguished by Wednesday night. The company denied the platform collapsed or that the fire caused an oil spill.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed a first-of-its-kind law banning the dilation and evacuation abortion procedure, commonly used in the second trimester. Supporters call it a groundbreaking pro-life measure; opponents say it is dangerous and among the most restrictive abortion laws in the US. Both sides are preparing to take the fight to other states and to court.

Chinese state TV host Bi Fujian has sparked controversy after a video surfaced showing him cursing Mao Zedong at a private dinner. Bi, who works for CCTV, later apologized on Weibo for his "improper speech" and the network said it would investigate. The video has divided Chinese social media, with some calling for harsh punishment and others defending him.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using a racial slur about Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky following the Wildcats' Final Four loss. Harrison, who is black, called the remark "in jest" and said he apologized directly to Kaminsky, who is white. Kaminsky said he was "over it" and that "nothing needs to be made out of it."

"Arrested Development" executive producer Brian Grazer says the show will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes. Netflix had no comment when asked to verify his statements. It was not yet known if the full cast will return.

The Large Hadron Collider restarted Sunday after a two-year shutdown, with beams circulating in its 27 km ring following final tests. CERN aims to recreate post-Big Bang conditions at record energy levels to probe dark matter, mass origins and other gaps in the Standard Model.

An Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of an armed U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf this month, raising U.S. concerns that Tehran's top commanders may not fully control local forces. The previously undisclosed incident occurred as U.S. and world powers negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran in Switzerland. U.S. officials believe the maneuver may have been locally ordered, and the administration is considering a demarche protest.

A jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, including 17 capital charges that make him eligible for the death penalty. The trial now moves to a penalty phase, where jurors will weigh aggravating and mitigating factors to decide whether Tsarnaev, 21, is executed. No start date has been set for the penalty phase.

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees after federal minister Smriti Irani found a security camera pointed at a store changing room in Goa. The store manager remains at large; the arrested face voyeurism and privacy breach charges carrying up to three years in jail. FabIndia says it is investigating and cooperating with police.

Iran will lift its ban on women attending some men's sports events next year, a deputy sports minister said. The ban, in place since 1979, will be eased for indoor events, though it is unclear which matches women may attend. The restrictions have drawn international pressure, including from FIFA.

An Indian court sentenced software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others to seven years in jail for their roles in the $1.6 billion Satyam Computer Services fraud. Raju, the company's former chairman, was also fined $804,000. He has been jailed for the past 32 months.

Elizabeth Sedway was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii after an employee noticed she was seated in the handicapped section and she said she sometimes felt weak. The airline said its policy is to consult medical professionals when a passenger has a health issue, but later apologized, refunded the family's tickets and paid for overnight accommodations. Sedway said the disruption caused her to miss chemotherapy and her children to miss school.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan died of cancer Friday in an Istanbul hospital at age 66, five days after his birthday. He was first diagnosed in 1990, the year he competed in Eurovision, and released his breakout album "I Made a Vow" in 1991. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu mourned the loss of an artist who "marked a generation."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the framework nuclear deal with Iran, arguing for increased pressure instead of "this bad deal or war." The deal, endorsed by President Obama, would limit Iran's centrifuges and uranium enrichment in exchange for lifted sanctions. Senate Democrat Dianne Feinstein urged Netanyahu to "contain himself," while Republicans argued a better deal could be reached under a new president.

Washington was rocked by connected shootings Thursday, beginning with a suspected domestic kidnapping that led to a guard being shot at the Census Bureau in Suitland, Maryland. A chase ended in a crash and shootout on H Street in Washington, wounding an officer and the suspect. The kidnapping victim was found in good condition.

Chelsea Manning, imprisoned for leaking classified documents, has joined Twitter. She will dictate tweets by phone to a communications firm since she lacks Internet access in prison. Manning is serving a 35-year sentence at Fort Leavenworth and was granted hormone therapy for gender dysphoria.

Rapper Nelly was arrested on drug charges in Tennessee after a state trooper pulled over his private bus on Interstate 40. Authorities said a search of the bus turned up methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia, handguns and Ziploc bags. Nelly, whose real name is Cornell Haynes, was jailed and later released on bond.

A Delaware father is improving while his two sons remain in critical condition after suspected pesticide exposure at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort. The EPA found methyl bromide, a restricted neurotoxin, in the family's rented villa. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation.

Online journalists across Asia face legal harassment and violence as governments and extremists target bloggers who operate outside state-controlled media. In Singapore and Malaysia, authorities use courts and arrests to silence dissent, while China and Vietnam lead the world in jailing bloggers and reporters. In Bangladesh, bloggers critical of Islam have been hacked to death with near-total impunity.

Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving "The Vampire Diaries" after the current sixth season, saying she always envisioned Elena's story as a six-season arc. Fans reacted angrily, blaming producers for continuing the CW show into a seventh season and fearing the end of the "Delena" romance. Producer Julie Plec said she supports Dobrev's decision and looks forward to continuing the series.

ISIS stormed the Yarmouk camp in Damascus two weeks ago, prompting Syrian government bombing and shelling that has flattened buildings and killed residents. Most fighters on all sides are Palestinians, with pro-government factions besieging the camp and anti-regime groups, including Islamists, holding the inside. Of the 100,000 residents who once lived there, only about 18,000 remain, with little aid allowed in or out.

NASA says signs of life on exoplanets will likely be found in coming decades using advanced telescopes. But communicating with intelligent aliens is unlikely anytime soon, given the tiny fraction of a planet's history that radio-capable life exists.

A Massachusetts man will be arraigned April 14 on a murder charge after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge. Carlos Colina, 32, was previously arraigned on charges of assault and improper disposal of a body. The remains were identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who authorities say knew Colina.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he assaulted at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2013. The settlement included an apology from West to Ramos, and the two shook hands, according to Ramos' attorney Gloria Allred. West had pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and received two years' probation, anger management and community service.

Obama's political legacy is deeply tied to securing a nuclear deal with Iran, leading to U.S. desperation in negotiations that has strengthened Iran's hand. The framework agreement allows Iran to retain thousands of centrifuges and lifts sanctions too soon, alarming Arab allies who fear Iran is outplaying the U.S. The deal provides Obama political cover but does little to prevent nuclear proliferation or Middle East instability.

A bystander's video of a white South Carolina officer fatally shooting an unarmed black man after a traffic stop led to the officer's swift arrest on murder charges. The case highlights a broader failure: a 1994 federal law requiring the Justice Department to collect data on police killings has never been implemented, leaving the true scope of such incidents unknown.

Five Americans monitored for Ebola exposure at an Omaha hospital have been released after none developed the virus. The clinicians were exposed in Sierra Leone in March while working for Partners in Health. More than 10,000 people have died in the West African Ebola epidemic since December 2013.

Mark Ronson and Bruno Mars' "Uptown Funk!" notches a 13th week atop the Billboard Hot 100, becoming the longest-running No. 1 of the 2010s and just the 10th single ever to spend at least 13 weeks at the top. The song also leads Digital Songs, Streaming Songs and Radio Songs simultaneously for a record-extending ninth week. Natalie La Rose's debut hit "Somebody," featuring Jeremih, enters the top 10 at No. 10.

April 8 marked both the "Lost" anniversary and "Rex Manning Day," honoring the 1995 film "Empire Records." Other notable film dates include April 14 ("Titanic"), April 25 ("Miss Congeniality"), October 3 ("Mean Girls") and October 21, 2015 ("Back to the Future Part II").

"Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman, will bypass U.S. theaters and premiere directly on Lifetime on May 25. The Weinstein Co. sold the critically-panned film, which opened Cannes last year, to the network after poor international performance.

Shibuya ward in Tokyo passed an ordinance allowing same-sex couples to obtain "partnership certificates," granting limited rights such as hospital visitation and co-signing tenancy agreements. The non-binding measure, a first for Japan, is seen as a step toward marriage equality, though national law would be needed for full equal rights.

California's historic drought is driving up national food prices, with berries, broccoli, grapes, melons, peppers and packaged salad all costing more in 2014. The drought, now in its fourth year, has prompted mandatory 25% water cutbacks and is expected to keep fruit and vegetable prices rising in 2015.

The University of Michigan will screen "American Sniper" after initially canceling it over student objections. More than 200 students had petitioned against the film, citing its portrayal of the Iraq War and the Middle East. A counter-petition followed, and the school's vice president for student life said canceling was "a mistake" inconsistent with free expression.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards delivered highlights including Amy Schumer's sharp opening monologue, Channing Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez, and a killer Fall Out Boy/Fetty Wap mashup. Misfires included Schumer's botched archery gag, a flat "Gone Girl" joke, and meandering speeches from Shailene Woodley and Zac Efron/Dave Franco.

A 20-30 foot section of fiberglass boat, suspected debris from the 2011 Japan tsunami, was towed into Newport, Oregon, this week. Inside were yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters. Biologists determined the invasive species threat was small; the fish will go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium and the boat remnants to a landfill.

One year after Boko Haram kidnapped nearly 300 schoolgirls from Chibok, Nigeria, more than 200 remain missing. President-elect Buhari pledged an aggressive effort to defeat the militants, but Boko Haram still controls swaths of the northeast. The #BringBackOurGirls hashtag continues to trend as families remain bereft.

Easter's Holy Week, culminating in the Easter Triduum of Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday, remains resistant to the commercialization and culture wars surrounding Christmas. The three-day arc from crucifixion to resurrection mirrors a universal human pattern of suffering, limbo and transformation that believers and nonbelievers alike experience repeatedly. The ritual reminds observers to expect the movement from darkness into light.

Kenya has frozen 86 accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following last week's Garissa university massacre that killed 147 people. The government is tracking suspect finances and launched airstrikes on Al-Shabaab camps in Somalia, while offering a $215,000 reward for the alleged attack organizer. Kenyans mourned the victims at Nairobi's Uhuru Park with 147 crosses and used #147notjustanumber to honor the dead.

Jia Jiang launched the "100 Days of Rejection" project after quitting his six-figure job to pursue entrepreneurship, confronting his fear of rejection through 100 challenges. His Krispy Kreme Olympic donut request went viral, leading to talk show appearances and his new book "Rejection Proof." Jiang now speaks across the US, aiming to help others turn rejection into opportunity.

Attorney General Eric Holder has prohibited all Justice Department employees from soliciting prostitutes, regardless of local legality, citing the link to human trafficking. The memo follows an inspector general report detailing DEA agents attending cartel-funded sex parties overseas. Violators face suspension or firing.

A Wayne Community College employee was shot and killed on campus Monday in what authorities say may have been a hate crime. The suspect, a former work-study student, was arrested Tuesday in Florida after fleeing the scene.

Amnesty International's annual review finds governments increasingly using the death penalty in misguided responses to crime and terrorism, citing China's mass sentencing in Xinjiang, Pakistan's post-Peshawar executions, and Iran and Iraq's terrorism-related executions. Global executions fell from 778 in 2013 to 607 in 2014, excluding China, though death sentences spiked by over 500 due to Egypt and Nigeria. Amnesty urges leaders to abandon capital punishment, noting 140 states are now abolitionist.

A Duke University student has admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near a campus student union, school officials said Thursday. The student, who was not identified, is no longer on campus and faces a student conduct review as criminal investigations continue. The incident sparked a campus march and forum, and follows other recent racist episodes at U.S. colleges.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor best known for playing senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law," has died at 86. He died Sunday at his Santa Monica home after a long illness, his wife said. Dysart won the 1992 Emmy for outstanding supporting actor in a drama series and appeared in every episode of the show's eight-season run.

Easter, which celebrates Christ's crucifixion and resurrection, falls on a different date each year because its timing is tied to the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox, a rule set at the Council of Nicaea in 325. Western and Orthodox Christians often celebrate on separate dates due to differing calendars, while secular traditions like the Easter bunny and colored eggs—likely brought to North America by German immigrants in the 1700s—remain popular trappings.

Comedian Chris Rock has tweeted about being stopped by police three times in seven weeks, highlighting the "driving while black" phenomenon. His posts drew support and criticism, including actor Isaiah Washington's advice to "#Adapt" by trading his Mercedes for a Prius. Blacks are about 30% more likely to be pulled over than whites, per 2013 Bureau of Justice Statistics figures.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., the original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday night in a single-car crash in Cartersville, Georgia, according to the Georgia State Patrol. He was 64. Burns, who left the band in 1975, was not restrained at the time of the crash.

A photo of a cat on stairs has sparked a social media debate over whether it is going up or down, reminiscent of #TheDress. The image, posted on Imgur and popularized on 9gag, has users debating the cat's motion and the stairs' construction. Advertisers are already capitalizing on the viral debate.

The US and P5+1 reached a framework agreement with Iran to limit its nuclear program and block weapons development. The deal reduces Iran's uranium stockpile, cuts centrifuges by two-thirds, and implements rigorous inspections. Critics' claims about the deal's objectives and sunset clauses are misleading, as the agreement's inspection provisions are permanent.

Rolling Stone retracted its story about an alleged gang rape at UVA, but the article's broader point remains undisputed: the university is under state and federal investigation for its handling of sexual assault and has never expelled a student for it. Survivors and advocates fear the retraction will discourage victims from coming forward, though UVA has since adopted a zero-tolerance policy.

Pacers forward Chris Copeland and a woman were stabbed outside a New York nightclub early Wednesday; Copeland is in stable condition. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges after the incident, though police say they were not involved in the stabbing. A suspect is in custody and charges are pending.

Twisted Sister has announced that its 2016 tour will be its last, titled "Forty and F*ck It" to mark the band's 40th anniversary. Singer Dee Snider confirmed the farewell on Facebook and said drummer Mike Portnoy will replace the late A.J. Pero, who died March 20. The band will play two shows in Pero's honor, in Las Vegas and Sayreville, New Jersey.

John Travolta says he has not seen and does not care to see HBO's new Scientology documentary "Going Clear." The actor, a high-profile church member, called Scientology "brilliant" and credited it with helping him survive his son's 2009 death. He dismissed the documentary as the product of "disgruntled" former members.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million opening weekend as fans mourned Paul Walker, who died before filming completed. The film retired Walker's character Brian in an emotional ending featuring a montage set to Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth's "See You Again." Social media users flooded Twitter and Facebook with messages about crying during the tribute.

"Game of Thrones" returns Sunday for its fifth season, airing simultaneously in 170 countries for the first time. Major story arcs will begin converging, with some moving ahead of George R.R. Martin's books. Arya, Sansa and Cersei are the characters to watch as the series builds toward its seven-season end.

A CNN roundup details several real-life cases of people surviving days, weeks or months stranded at sea, including Louis Jordan, rescued off North Carolina after 66 days; Jose Salvador Alvarenga, who drifted from Mexico to the Marshall Islands over 13 months; and Ron Ingraham, picked up near Honolulu after 12 days. Other cases include Panamanian teenager Adrian Vasquez, adrift 26 days before being rescued near the Galapagos, and Hiromitsu Shinkawa, who clung to debris for two days after Japan's 2011 tsunami. Such survival stories are rare, with fatal outcomes far more common.

The first six "Star Wars" films arrive on digital HD Friday with extensive special features. The extras include behind-the-scenes looks at the saga's sound effects, such as the Geonosians' alien sounds in "Attack of the Clones." Sound designer Ben Burtt explains which animals were used to create the effects.

Jurors found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts Wednesday for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings and their aftermath. Survivors and victims' families welcomed the verdict as accountability and a step toward closure, though many said true justice is impossible. The trial now moves to the penalty phase, where Tsarnaev could face the death penalty.

China formally charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets on Friday, making him the highest-ranking Communist Party official ever to face corruption charges. Zhou, 72, a former Politburo Standing Committee member who retired in 2012, will be tried in Tianjin.

A Philadelphia woman was charged Sunday after allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in Cobbs Creek Park for more than four days while she traveled to Maryland to visit her boyfriend. The man, who has cerebral palsy and cannot communicate, was found with only a blanket and a Bible and was hospitalized with dehydration, malnutrition and an infected cut. The mother faces charges including aggravated assault, kidnapping and neglect of a care-dependent person.

Walmart's opposition to Arkansas' religious freedom bill pressured Gov. Asa Hutchinson to seek changes to the legislation, highlighting the retailer's emergence as a bellwether on divisive social issues. The backlash from major companies against similar laws in Indiana and Arkansas underscores growing business support for gay equality, with some Republicans urging the GOP to adapt.

A lapsed Catholic recounts how Pope Francis reawakened her faith after a church rejected her when she sought a priest following her brother's death. She credits Francis' tone of inclusion and non-judgment, exemplified by his "who am I to judge?" remark on homosexuality. A newly appointed cardinal tells her the church should have "an open heart," welcoming all without imposing its teachings.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau, whose affair began when she was his 34-year-old teacher and he was 13, say they remain happily married. The couple, who wed in 2005 and have two teen daughters, will mark their 10th anniversary May 20. They discuss their marriage, her plans to teach again and his struggles with alcoholism in an ABC "20/20" interview airing Friday.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign will serve as a referendum on gender equality in the US, a burden no male candidate would face. Her win or loss will be overinterpreted as a verdict on women in politics, though partisanship and her unique profile—not sexism—will likely determine the outcome.

Amnesty International's annual report accuses governments worldwide of using the death penalty to combat real or perceived terrorism threats. Global executions fell 22% to at least 607 in 2014, but death sentences rose 28% to 2,466, driven by mass sentencings in Egypt and Nigeria. The U.S. was the only country in the Americas to carry out executions, with 35, behind Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia.

Japan's defense minister told parliament the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered a UFO from outer space, responding to a query from lawmaker and former wrestler Antonio Inoki. Inoki, who claims to have seen a UFO himself, asked whether jets had been scrambled over extraterrestrial threats.

Mark Wahlberg will star in "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films production about the Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt, Deadline reported. Wahlberg hopes to play then-Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis, with the story told from his perspective. It is the second film announced about the 2013 attack, following Fox's "Boston Strong."

Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, both weighing long-shot Democratic presidential bids, showcased contrasting campaign styles at an Iowa dinner Friday. O'Malley worked the room with selfies and handshakes, while Webb stayed seated and delivered a subdued speech. Both trail Hillary Clinton badly in polls ahead of her expected Sunday announcement.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested Wednesday at the Turkey-Syria border on suspicion of attempting to cross illegally into Syria, the Turkish military said. All nine held British passports, according to a Turkish official. The UK Foreign Office said it is seeking information from Turkish authorities.

The Justice Department has indicted FedEx on 15 counts, alleging the courier knowingly shipped controlled substances for illegal online pharmacies. FedEx argues it is a common carrier exempt from possession laws and cannot be held liable for sealed packages it transports. The case tests whether corporations can be criminally prosecuted for the actions of customers.

Kenyans used the hashtag #147notjustanumber to share victims' stories after Al-Shabaab's attack on Garissa University College killed 147 people, mostly students. The attack was Kenya's deadliest since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing, and churches mourned the dead on Easter Sunday. Authorities identified one attacker as the son of a Mandera government official who had reported him missing.

Sweden offers 480 days of parental leave, with 60 "daddy months" reserved for fathers that are lost if unused. Photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers who take full advantage of the policy, though only 12% of Swedish couples share the leave equally. Bavman seeks 60 fathers for an exhibition and book, having found 35 so far.

Obama tells the New York Times he is "absolutely committed" to maintaining Israel's military edge over Iran amid Netanyahu's criticism of the Iran nuclear deal. He says he would commit to defending Israel if attacked by any state, calling the deal a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" to take the nuclear issue off the table. The framework would cut Iran's centrifuges from 19,000 to 5,060, with final talks set to continue until June 30.

States have enacted religious freedom laws since 1993, with Indiana's new RFRA sparking debate over whether such measures protect faith or enable discrimination against gay people. Experts say state RFRA claims are rare and mostly favor religious minorities. Notable cases include Native American eagle feathers, a Brazilian sacramental tea, kosher prison meals, a Sikh kirpan and Chicago church zoning.

Five Chinese feminists detained in March face up to five years in prison after police recommended charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order." Prosecutors must decide by Monday whether to pursue the charges against the Women's Rights Action Group members, whose detention has drawn international criticism.

Tejano star Selena, who died 20 years ago, will be revived as a "walking, talking, singing and dancing digital embodiment" called "Selena the One," her family announced. The hologram-like figure, created by Nevada tech company Acrovirt LLC, will release new music, collaborate with current artists and tour in 2018. An Indiegogo campaign launching April 16 aims to raise $500,000 for the project.

Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz over his Iran nuclear negotiations, writing on Facebook that Obama is flying the nation "into the rocks." The former Minnesota congresswoman's comments drew widespread criticism from Facebook users who called the analogy despicable and disrespectful.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River," divisive since its Cannes premiere, opens in limited U.S. and UK release April 10. Gosling says the film grew out of speculative footage he shot of Detroit's soon-to-be-demolished Brewster-Douglass Projects. He describes the city as both decaying and undergoing a rebirth, a paradox the film aims to capture.

A 19-year-old UK national was charged with terror offenses after being arrested at Luton airport upon returning from Turkey. Yahya Rashid, from northwest London, faces charges of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others to commit them between November 1 and March 31. He is due in Westminster Magistrates' Court Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe's Vince Neil delivered a widely panned rendition of the national anthem before a Las Vegas Outlaws arena football game, joining a long list of famous anthem performances ranging from Whitney Houston's celebrated 1991 Super Bowl version to Roseanne Barr's booed 1990 outing. Jimi Hendrix's psychedelic 1969 Woodstock take and Michael Bolton's lyric-flubbing 2003 performance round out the notable hits and misses.

Nearly 2,000 WWI soldiers' graffiti inscriptions have been discovered in an underground city beneath battlefields near Naours, France. The site, sealed in the 18th century and reopened in 2013, contains names of mostly Australian and British troops, including 55 Americans. Photographer Jeff Gusky, who has documented 1,821 names, calls the find a "treasure trove" connecting the present to men who fought a century ago.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The ICC opened a preliminary examination in January into possible war crimes, including against Israelis, though Palestinians may face counter-charges. Israel and the US, neither of which is an ICC member, opposed the move.

Anthony Ray Hinton walked free Friday after nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row for 1985 murders he maintained he did not commit. A judge dismissed the charges after the state declined to re-prosecute following expert testimony that the gun in the case could not be matched to evidence. Hinton, 58, said he lost three decades of his life to an unjust conviction and that those responsible will "answer to God."

Most American taxpayers receive refunds averaging nearly $3,000, and free filing services have made Tax Day a happy spending spree rather than a dreaded chore. But the U.S. tax system remains deeply flawed—biased against two-earner couples, overly complex, and favoring the rich who earn from capital rather than wages. Happy endings, as Kahneman's research shows, help taxpayers forget the unpleasantness that came before.

Jordan Spieth takes a four-shot lead into the final round of the Masters after a steady third round at Augusta. Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose, Rory McIlroy and Tiger Woods all made moves but failed to significantly close the gap. Spieth's late double bogey at 17 offered the chasing pack faint hope of a comeback.

Liana Barrientos, 39, has been married 10 times—nine times between 1999 and 2002—and is accused of falsifying a 2010 marriage license application as part of an immigration scam. She pleaded not guilty Friday in Bronx State Supreme Court and faces up to four years in prison if convicted. After leaving court, she was arrested for allegedly sneaking into the New York subway through an emergency exit.

An Indiana pizzeria faced backlash and threats after saying it would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding under the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Critics called for boycotts, but supporters donated more than $842,000 to the owners via GoFundMe. Police recommended charges over a tweet threatening to burn down the restaurant.

Vijay Chokalingam, brother of actress Mindy Kaling, revealed he posed as an African-American on medical school applications in the 1990s to expose affirmative action, an act his sister said brought "shame upon their family." Despite the ruse, he received only one acceptance, from St. Louis University, while Harvard, Penn and Columbia rejected him. He now plans a book titled "Almost Black."

Antarctica may have recorded its highest temperature ever on March 24, with a reading of 63.5 degrees Fahrenheit (15.5 Celsius) at Argentina's Esperanza Base. The World Meteorological Organization is forming a committee to verify the measurement. Researchers studying climate change closely monitor Antarctic weather for warming evidence.

The Obama administration said Thursday it is "not putting a timeframe on" a possible Iraqi-led invasion to retake Mosul, nearly three months after a U.S. official said up to 25,000 Iraqi troops were expected to return to the key northern city in April or May. Officials stressed that Iraqi forces and their allies are making progress against ISIS, including the recent recapture of Tikrit, but warned that winning Mosul is a complex endeavor that will take time to build.

Paddy Power has deleted a tweet that joked Newcastle had "suffered more Kop beatings over the last 20 years than an unarmed African-American male." The Irish betting company said "no offense was meant," but social media users condemned the post and some called for the writer to be sacked. Liverpool beat Newcastle 2-0 Monday at Anfield.

Philadelphia police have added attempted murder to charges against Nyia Parler, accused of leaving her quadriplegic 21-year-old son in a park for days while she traveled to Maryland. Parler, 41, remains in custody in Maryland receiving unspecified treatment and cannot be extradited until it is complete. The son was found Friday in Cobbs Creek Park with a Bible and wheelchair nearby, suffering dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries.

A South Korean court charged Kim Ki-Jong with attempted murder, assaulting a foreign envoy and business obstruction for stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul last month. Lippert was slashed in the face and arm during a March 5 event and required 80 stitches, but suffered no serious nerve damage. Kim, who has a history of unpredictable behavior, opposed joint South Korean-U.S. military drills.
Jill (Duggar) Dillard, the first daughter married from "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth Monday to a 9-pound, 10-ounce son named Israel David. The baby arrived more than a week past his due date.

"Furious 7" is eyeing a $135 million-$138 million domestic debut, the largest North American opening since fall 2013, with a projected $58 million-$60 million Friday gross. The Universal film, the last featuring the late Paul Walker, also earned a record-breaking $60 million internationally Wednesday and Thursday, with a worldwide debut potentially nearing or crossing $300 million by Easter Sunday. It opens in 4,003 domestic theaters and more than 10,500 international screens in 63 territories.

The Secret Service is facing a new scandal after a female employee accused supervisor Xavier Morales of assault following sexual advances at a March 31 party. Morales has been placed on administrative leave and had his security clearance suspended. The incident adds to a series of recent high-profile missteps at the agency and will be investigated by the Office of the Inspector General.

Hillary Clinton is announcing her 2016 presidential candidacy, bringing extensive experience but facing questions about authenticity, inevitability and voter enthusiasm. Her campaign plans smaller events to connect directly with voters, as she must articulate a compelling vision and address Democratic base concerns. She also must manage challenges including gender bias, her husband's role and Clinton Foundation scrutiny.

The Justice Department will begin negotiations with Ferguson to restructure its police department after a report found a pattern of racial discrimination. The city has already seen leadership changes, including the resignations of its city manager and police chief, and the election of two black city council members. The scope of change will depend on continued activism as the DOJ talks proceed.

An Etihad Airways flight from Abu Dhabi to New York lost a passenger's pet cat after its carrier was damaged, allowing the animal to escape on the grounds of JFK Airport. The cat, Felix, remains missing nearly a week later as the airline investigates and works with ground handlers and third-party specialists to locate him. The owners, who paid $1,200 to ship the cat during their relocation, say they will continue searching until they have answers.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued Thursday by the crew of a container ship after drifting in his disabled sailboat for 66 days in the Atlantic Ocean. He survived by collecting rainwater and catching fish with a hand net after his boat capsized and his mast broke. Coast Guard officials say they have found no reason to doubt his story.
